questions.title: Above Department Average
questions.description:
The CTO wants employees who out-earn their own department's average. Build the per-department averages in a CTE, then join it back to the base table.

Schema:
- employees(id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, name TEXT, manager_id INTEGER -> employees.id, department TEXT, salary INTEGER)

Twelve employees are seeded in three departments (Executive, Engineering, Sales). Dana Whitfield is the CEO with manager_id NULL. Reporting chains run four levels deep, e.g. Dana -> Alex Kim -> Rosa Alvarez -> Lena Fischer. Salaries are whole dollars; the company average salary is 131750.

Task:
Build a CTE holding each department's average salary, then join it back to employees on department and keep only the employees who out-earn their own department's average. Return e.name AS employee_name, e.salary AS salary and the department average rounded to two decimals AS dept_avg, ordered by salary descending, then employee_name ascending.

Rules:
- SQLite dialect. The schema and its data are pre-seeded automatically — do not include CREATE TABLE or INSERT statements in your answer.
- Column names and order must match exactly (alias every output column).
- Row order must match exactly (use ORDER BY as specified).

  name TEXT NOT NULL,
  manager_id INTEGER,
  department TEXT NOT NULL,
  salary INTEGER NOT NULL
);

questions.title: Cap the Bonus at 4500
questions.description:

questions.title: Chain Salary Roll Up
questions.description:
The recursion accumulates: starting from the CEO's salary, each step adds the employee's own salary, so every chain from the top carries a running total down to that person.

Schema:
- employees(id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, name TEXT, manager_id INTEGER -> employees.id, department TEXT, salary INTEGER)

Walk the org chart with a recursive CTE that accumulates salary: the anchor seeds the CEO (NULL manager_id) with their own salary at depth 1, and every recursive step adds the next employee's salary to the running total carried down the chain. Schema:

Schema:

Task:

2) Mark the run as fully processed: set processed = 3 in payroll_runs (three Engineering employees).
3) Finish with a SELECT returning name and bonus for employees where dept = 'Engineering', ordered by name ascending.

- SQLite dialect. The schema and its data are pre-seeded automatically — do not include CREATE TABLE statements in your answer.
- Multi-statement task: run the statements in the numbered order, then finish with ONE final SELECT — only that last result set is graded.
- Every statement before the final SELECT must produce no rows (UPDATE and INSERT without RETURNING are silent).
- Column names and order must match exactly (alias every output column).
- Row order must match exactly (use ORDER BY as specified).

questions.description:
The board wants every agent's total portfolio value — agents without listings must appear with 0, so a LEFT JOIN against a derived table is required. No CTEs on this one.

Schema:

questions.title: Idempotent Sales Re-Run
questions.description:
A production-grade procedure is idempotent: running it twice must not double the bonus. The pct body carries its own guard — it only writes when the current bonus is BELOW the target — and the script executes the identical statement twice, then stamps the run with the number of Sales employees processed.

Schema:

Money is whole dollars; SQLite has no CREATE PROCEDURE, so each 'procedure' below is a multi-statement script executed in order.

Task:
1) Execute: for every employee whose dept = 'Sales' AND bonus < (base_salary / 100) * 5, set bonus = (base_salary / 100) * 5.
2) Execute that exact same statement a second time (it must be a no-op now).
3) Set processed = 2 in payroll_runs.
4) Finish with a SELECT returning name and bonus for employees where dept = 'Sales', ordered by name ascending — the bonuses must match a single execution.

Rules:
- SQLite dialect. The schema and its data are pre-seeded automatically — do not include CREATE TABLE statements in your answer.
- Multi-statement task: run the statements in the numbered order, then finish with ONE final SELECT — only that last result set is graded.
- Every statement before the final SELECT must produce no rows (UPDATE and INSERT without RETURNING are silent).
- Column names and order must match exactly (alias every output column).
- Row order must match exactly (use ORDER BY as specified).

questions.title: Interclub Fixture Ledger
questions.description:
The hall office combines a full cross join of players with a hall lookup so every interclub fixture shows the home player's hall.

Schema:
- players(id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, name TEXT, club TEXT, rating INTEGER)
- club_halls(club TEXT, hall TEXT) -> players.club
- rounds(round_no INTEGER)
- openings(id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, opening TEXT)
- games(id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, round_no INTEGER, white_id INTEGER -> players.id, black_id INTEGER -> players.id, white_score REAL)

Eight players across four clubs (Kings, Rooks, Bishops, Knights) are seeded; Vera Holt and Sana Qadir share the top rating 2410. Each club has exactly one hall. Five rounds and five openings are defined. Six games have been played (white_score is the white player's points: 1 win, 0.5 draw, 0 loss).

questions.description:
For the interclub league, every player must appear as home against every player from a different club.

Schema:
- players(id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, name TEXT, club TEXT, rating INTEGER)

- rounds(round_no INTEGER)
- openings(id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, opening TEXT)

questions.title: Interest Posting With a Savepoint
questions.description:
Savings accounts earn 2% interest. The posting is fenced by a savepoint that is released, then committed — a small-scale atomic batch.

Schema:
- accounts(id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, holder TEXT, balance INTEGER, kind TEXT)

Six accounts are seeded; balance is stored in integer cents (250000 means 2,500.00) and kind is 'checking' or 'savings'. All amounts in your script are integer cents too.

Task:
1) Start a transaction with BEGIN.
2) Create a savepoint named s1.
3) Update every account where kind = 'savings': set balance = balance + (balance / 100) * 2 (integer cents arithmetic).
4) Fold the savepoint away with RELEASE s1.
5) Commit with COMMIT.
6) Finish with a SELECT returning id, holder and balance for the savings accounts only (kind = 'savings'), ordered by id ascending.

Rules:
- SQLite dialect. The schema and its data are pre-seeded automatically — do not include CREATE TABLE statements in your answer.
- Multi-statement task: run the transaction statements in the listed order, then finish with ONE final SELECT — only that last result set is graded.
- Every statement before the final SELECT must produce no rows (BEGIN, COMMIT, ROLLBACK, SAVEPOINT and UPDATE are all silent).
- Column names and order must match exactly (alias every output column).
- Row order must match exactly (use ORDER BY as specified).

How busy was everyone? Each player's games must be counted whether they played white or black, and their points totalled (black receives 1 - white_score).

Schema:
- players(id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, name TEXT, club TEXT, rating INTEGER)
- club_halls(club TEXT, hall TEXT) -> players.club
- rounds(round_no INTEGER)
- openings(id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, opening TEXT)
- games(id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, round_no INTEGER, white_id INTEGER -> players.id, black_id INTEGER -> players.id, white_score REAL)

Eight players across four clubs (Kings, Rooks, Bishops, Knights) are seeded; Vera Holt and Sana Qadir share the top rating 2410. Each club has exactly one hall. Five rounds and five openings are defined. Six games have been played (white_score is the white player's points: 1 win, 0.5 draw, 0 loss).

Task:
Join players p to games g ON g.white_id = p.id OR g.black_id = p.id, group by player, and return p.name AS player_name, COUNT(g.id) AS games_played and ROUND(SUM(CASE WHEN g.white_id = p.id THEN g.white_score ELSE 1.0 - g.white_score END), 2) AS points, ordered by points descending, then player_name ascending.

Rules:
- SQLite dialect. The schema and its data are pre-seeded automatically — do not include CREATE TABLE or INSERT statements in your answer.
- Column names and order must match exactly (alias every output column).
- Row order must match exactly (use ORDER BY as specified).

questions.title: Podium Shortlists
questions.description:
Each race publishes a podium shortlist of its three fastest finishers. Row-number inside a CTE, then filter — window functions cannot be filtered directly in WHERE.

Schema:
- runners(id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, name TEXT, country TEXT)
- results(id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, runner_id INTEGER -> runners.id, category TEXT, finish_seconds INTEGER)

Ten runners are seeded; nine ran the full marathon and seven the half (five runners ran both). finish_seconds are whole seconds; category is 'full' or 'half'. Deliberate ties exist inside each category: full has three pairs (7620, 7935, 8100) and half has one pair (4380).

Task:
WITH ranked AS (join results res to runners r; select r.name AS runner_name, res.category AS category and ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY res.category ORDER BY res.finish_seconds, res.runner_id) AS position) — return category AS category, position AS position and runner_name AS runner_name FROM ranked WHERE position <= 3, ordered by category ascending, then position ascending.

Rules:
- SQLite dialect. The schema and its data are pre-seeded automatically — do not include CREATE TABLE or INSERT statements in your answer.
- Column names and order must match exactly (alias every window column).
- Row order must match exactly (use ORDER BY as specified).

questions.title: Pre and Post Snapshots
questions.description:
Compliance wants BOTH a before-image and an after-image per change. Two triggers share one UPDATE: the BEFORE trigger logs the pre-change snapshot, the AFTER trigger logs the post-change confirmation.

Schema:
- items(id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, sku TEXT, quantity INTEGER, price REAL)
- audit_log(id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, action TEXT, item_sku TEXT, old_qty INTEGER, new_qty INTEGER, changed_at TEXT)

Eight items are seeded; audit_log starts EMPTY — every row you will see in it is produced by the trigger(s) you create. Never use date('now'): write fixed literal dates such as '2026-01-15' for changed_at.

Task:
1) Create a trigger named t_pre_snapshot: BEFORE UPDATE ON items, INSERTing an audit row with action 'before-update', item_sku = OLD.sku, old_qty = OLD.quantity, new_qty = NEW.quantity, changed_at = '2026-01-25'.
2) Create a trigger named t_post_snapshot: AFTER UPDATE ON items, INSERTing an audit row with action 'after-update' and the same NEW/OLD values and date.
3) UPDATE the item with id 3 to quantity = 70.
4) Finish with a SELECT returning action, old_qty and new_qty from audit_log, ordered by id ascending — exactly two rows.

Rules:
- SQLite dialect. The schema and its data are pre-seeded automatically — do not include CREATE TABLE or INSERT INTO items statements in your answer.
- Multi-statement task: create the trigger(s) first, then run the listed DML statements, then finish with ONE final SELECT — only that last result set is graded.
- Every statement before the final SELECT must produce no rows (CREATE TRIGGER and DML are silent; the trigger's inserts happen inside the engine).
- Trigger bodies wrap their INSERT statements in BEGIN … END with a semicolon after END.
- Column names and order must match exactly (alias every output column); row order must match exactly (use ORDER BY as specified).

questions.title: Quantity-Only Watch
questions.description:
Price tweaks should NOT hit the audit trail — only quantity changes. SQLite supports column-scoped triggers: AFTER UPDATE OF quantity ON items fires only when quantity appears in the statement's SET list.

Schema:
- items(id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, sku TEXT, quantity INTEGER, price REAL)
- audit_log(id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, action TEXT, item_sku TEXT, old_qty INTEGER, new_qty INTEGER, changed_at TEXT)

Eight items are seeded; audit_log starts EMPTY — every row you will see in it is produced by the trigger(s) you create. Never use date('now'): write fixed literal dates such as '2026-01-15' for changed_at.

Task:
1) Create a trigger named t_qty_only: AFTER UPDATE OF quantity ON items, whose body INSERTs one audit_log row with action 'update', item_sku = NEW.sku, old_qty = OLD.quantity, new_qty = NEW.quantity and changed_at = '2026-01-24'.
2) UPDATE the item with id 8: set price = 100.0 only (this must NOT fire the trigger).
3) UPDATE the item with id 8: set quantity = 20 and price = 60.0 (this must fire exactly once).
4) Finish with a SELECT returning action, item_sku, old_qty and new_qty from audit_log, ordered by id ascending.

Rules:
- SQLite dialect. The schema and its data are pre-seeded automatically — do not include CREATE TABLE or INSERT INTO items statements in your answer.
- Multi-statement task: create the trigger(s) first, then run the listed DML statements, then finish with ONE final SELECT — only that last result set is graded.
- Every statement before the final SELECT must produce no rows (CREATE TRIGGER and DML are silent; the trigger's inserts happen inside the engine).
- Trigger bodies wrap their INSERT statements in BEGIN … END with a semicolon after END.
- Column names and order must match exactly (alias every output column); row order must match exactly (use ORDER BY as specified).

Finance builds a per-room revenue view (rooms LEFT JOIN bookings so unbooked rooms still appear with zero revenue) and then triages: only rooms whose total revenue exceeds 500 make the escalation list.

Schema:
- rooms(id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, number TEXT, floor INTEGER, kind TEXT, nightly_rate REAL)
- bookings(id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, room_id INTEGER -> rooms.id, guest TEXT, check_in TEXT, nights INTEGER)

Eight rooms across four floors are seeded (kinds: standard, deluxe, suite, penthouse) plus ten bookings; Alice Grant, Brian Osei and Elena Petrova each book more than once, and room 103 has no bookings. Rates are USD per night.

Task:
1) Create a view named v_room_revenue that joins rooms (alias r) LEFT JOIN bookings (alias b) ON b.room_id = r.id and returns r.number aliased as number plus ROUND(IFNULL(SUM(r.nightly_rate * b.nights), 0), 2) aliased as total_revenue, grouped by r.id and r.number.
2) Finish with a SELECT from v_room_revenue returning number and total_revenue, but only where total_revenue > 500, ordered by total_revenue descending, tie-break by number ascending.

Rules:
- SQLite dialect. The rooms and bookings tables are pre-seeded automatically — do not include CREATE TABLE or INSERT statements in your answer.
- Multi-statement task: create the required view(s) first, then finish with ONE final SELECT — only that last result set is graded.
- Every statement before the final SELECT must produce no rows (CREATE VIEW is silent).
- Column names and order must match exactly (alias every output column).
- Row order must match exactly (use ORDER BY as specified).

CREATE VIEW v_room_revenue AS SELECT r.number AS number, ROUND(IFNULL(SUM(r.nightly_rate * b.nights), 0), 2) AS total_revenue FROM rooms r LEFT JOIN bookings b ON b.room_id = r.id GROUP BY r.id, r.number;

questions.title: Rollback Only the Failed Leg
questions.description:
The nightly batch posts two changes: a 120.00 referral credit to every savings account (approved), and a draft 9999.99 "loyalty correction" on every checking account (rejected). The correction is fenced in its own savepoint, rolled back, replaced by the approved 25.00 adjustment, and the batch commits once.

Schema:
- accounts(id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, holder TEXT, balance INTEGER, kind TEXT)

Six accounts are seeded; balance is stored in integer cents (250000 means 2,500.00) and kind is 'checking' or 'savings'. All amounts in your script are integer cents too.

Task:
1) Start a transaction with BEGIN.
2) Create a savepoint named s_ref and add 12000 cents to every account where kind = 'savings'; then fold it away with RELEASE s_ref.
3) Create a savepoint named s_loyal and subtract 999999 cents from every account where kind = 'checking'; then undo it with ROLLBACK TO s_loyal.
4) Subtract 2500 cents from every account where kind = 'checking' (the approved adjustment).
5) Commit with COMMIT.
6) Finish with a SELECT returning id, holder and balance for ALL accounts, ordered by id ascending.

Rules:
- SQLite dialect. The schema and its data are pre-seeded automatically — do not include CREATE TABLE statements in your answer.
- Multi-statement task: run the transaction statements in the listed order, then finish with ONE final SELECT — only that last result set is graded.
- Every statement before the final SELECT must produce no rows (BEGIN, COMMIT, ROLLBACK, SAVEPOINT and UPDATE are all silent).
- Column names and order must match exactly (alias every output column).
- Row order must match exactly (use ORDER BY as specified).

The same SKU moves twice in one session — the audit log must show every hop with its own old/new pair, plus the unrelated third move.

2) UPDATE the item with id 2 to quantity = 30.
3) UPDATE the item with id 2 to quantity = 22 (the second hop starts from 30).

Task:

questions.title: Three Trigger Types Together
questions.description:
The full audit suite: one trigger per DML event on items, all sharing the same log. Then one mixed shift exercises all three — update, delete, insert — and the trail must show the exact order they ran.

Schema:
- items(id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, sku TEXT, quantity INTEGER, price REAL)
- audit_log(id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, action TEXT, item_sku TEXT, old_qty INTEGER, new_qty INTEGER, changed_at TEXT)

Eight items are seeded; audit_log starts EMPTY — every row you will see in it is produced by the trigger(s) you create. Never use date('now'): write fixed literal dates such as '2026-01-15' for changed_at.

Task:
1) Create t_h_insert: AFTER INSERT ON items — action 'insert', item_sku = NEW.sku, old_qty = NULL, new_qty = NEW.quantity, changed_at = '2026-02-01'.
2) Create t_h_update: AFTER UPDATE ON items — action 'update', item_sku = NEW.sku, old_qty = OLD.quantity, new_qty = NEW.quantity, changed_at = '2026-02-01'.
3) Create t_h_delete: AFTER DELETE ON items — action 'delete', item_sku = OLD.sku, old_qty = OLD.quantity, new_qty = NULL, changed_at = '2026-02-01'.
4) UPDATE the item with id 1 to quantity = 44.
5) DELETE the item with id 8.
6) INSERT a new item: sku 'WH-9001', quantity 10, price 15.0.
7) Finish with a SELECT returning action, item_sku, old_qty and new_qty from audit_log, ordered by id ascending.

- SQLite dialect. The schema and its data are pre-seeded automatically — do not include CREATE TABLE or INSERT INTO items statements in your answer.
- Multi-statement task: create the trigger(s) first, then run the listed DML statements, then finish with ONE final SELECT — only that last result set is graded.
- Every statement before the final SELECT must produce no rows (CREATE TRIGGER and DML are silent; the trigger's inserts happen inside the engine).
- Trigger bodies wrap their INSERT statements in BEGIN … END with a semicolon after END.

Schema:

questions.title: Top Earner Per Department
questions.description:
Find each department's top earner: one CTE computes the MAX salary per department, then join back to employees on both department and salary. No window functions allowed.

Schema:
- employees(id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, name TEXT, manager_id INTEGER -> employees.id, department TEXT, salary INTEGER)

Compute each department's highest salary in a CTE (window functions are blacklisted, so no OVER), then join it back to employees on both department and salary to return e.name AS employee_name, e.department AS department and e.salary AS salary for each department's top earner, ordered by salary descending.

questions.title: Wire With Its Ledger Trail
questions.description:
A compliant wire writes the balance legs AND the ledger trail in one transaction — either both land or neither does. Move 250.00 from Bo Chen (id 2) to Amara Diallo (id 1), then finish by reading the joined ledger trail.

Schema:
- accounts(id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, holder TEXT, balance INTEGER, kind TEXT)
- ledger(id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, account_id INTEGER -> accounts.id, delta INTEGER, note TEXT)

Six accounts are seeded (balances in integer cents; kind is 'checking' or 'savings'). The ledger table exists but starts EMPTY — rows land in it only when your script inserts them.

Task:
1) Start a transaction with BEGIN.
2) Subtract 25000 cents from the account with id 2.
3) Add 25000 cents to the account with id 1.
4) Insert two ledger rows in ONE INSERT statement: (account_id 2, delta -25000, note 'wire out to Amara Diallo') and (account_id 1, delta 25000, note 'wire in from Bo Chen').
5) Commit with COMMIT.
6) Finish with a SELECT joining accounts (alias a) to ledger (alias l) ON l.account_id = a.id, returning a.holder aliased as holder, a.balance aliased as balance, l.note aliased as note and l.delta aliased as delta, ordered by l.id ascending.

Rules:
- SQLite dialect. The schema and its data are pre-seeded automatically — do not include CREATE TABLE statements in your answer.
- Multi-statement task: run the transaction statements in the listed order, then finish with ONE final SELECT — only that last result set is graded.
- Every statement before the final SELECT must produce no rows (BEGIN, COMMIT, ROLLBACK, SAVEPOINT and UPDATE are all silent).
- Column names and order must match exactly (alias every output column).
- Row order must match exactly (use ORDER BY as specified).

mcqQuestions.Option1: They avoid case-sensitivity and quoting headaches and stay readable

mcqQuestions.title: Why ROUND Money
mcqQuestions.description: Why wrap money aggregates in ROUND(x, 2)?
mcqQuestions.Option2: Averages produce long float tails; ROUND(..., 2) renders clean cents

mcqQuestions.title: Why Self Joins Need Aliases
mcqQuestions.description: Why must a self join give the two copies of a table different aliases?
mcqQuestions.Option2: Because aliases are required by COUNT
mcqQuestions.Option3: So each copy can be referenced by a distinct name
mcqQuestions.Option4: To hide the table name from users

mcqQuestions.title: Why Serve Views
mcqQuestions.description: Best reason an operations team exposes views instead of base tables to applications?
mcqQuestions.Option1: Restrict visible columns and rows and shield schema changes behind a stable interface
mcqQuestions.Option2: Views are always faster than base tables
mcqQuestions.Option3: Views store an extra copy that serves as backup
mcqQuestions.Option4: Views disable locking on the base tables

mcqQuestions.title: Why TRUNCATE Is Fast
mcqQuestions.description: In engines that have a real TRUNCATE statement, it is faster than a row-by-row DELETE because it…
mcqQuestions.Option4: Deallocates storage pages instead of scanning rows

mcqQuestions.title: Window Function In CTE Snippet
mcqQuestions.description: What does this statement return?
mcqQuestions.Option2: An error — WHERE cannot see rn
mcqQuestions.codesnippet:
WITH ranked AS (
  SELECT name, ROW_NUMBER() OVER (
    ORDER BY finish_seconds) AS rn
  FROM results)
SELECT name FROM ranked WHERE rn <= 3;

mcqQuestions.title: Window In WHERE
mcqQuestions.description: WHERE ROW_NUMBER() OVER (...) = 1 — why does this fail?
mcqQuestions.Option2: Window functions cannot be evaluated in WHERE — use a CTE or subquery to filter on the number
mcqQuestions.Option3: It runs but returns all rows

mcqQuestions.title: Window Versus GROUP BY
mcqQuestions.description: Unlike GROUP BY, window functions:
mcqQuestions.Option1: Collapse rows into one per group
mcqQuestions.Option2: Keep every row while adding per-window values

mcqQuestions.title: group_concat Default Separator
mcqQuestions.description: With no second argument, what separator does group_concat use?
mcqQuestions.codesnippet: SELECT group_concat(donor) FROM donations;

mcqQuestions.title: group_concat Order Caveat
mcqQuestions.description: What is guaranteed about the order of values inside group_concat output?
mcqQuestions.Option3: Not guaranteed — feed it an ORDER BY-ed subquery when order matters

mcqQuestions.title: sqlite3 CLI Table List
mcqQuestions.description: In the sqlite3 command-line client, which dot-command lists the database's tables?

mcqQuestions.title: sqlite_master Role
mcqQuestions.description: In SQLite, the sqlite_master table holds…
mcqQuestions.Option1: The data rows of user tables
mcqQuestions.Option4: The catalog of database objects such as tables and indexes
